name: CI
on:
  push:
  pull_request:

jobs:

    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5

          python eval/run_eval.py | tee -a "$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY"

chunks.title: deploy-render.yml
chunks.text:
# Redeploys the server on Render whenever the app code changes.
# Uses Render's deploy hook, stored as the repository secret RENDER_DEPLOY_HOOK
# (Render dashboard -> yakov-llm -> Settings -> Deploy Hook). Without it, does nothing.
name: Deploy to Render
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
    paths: ["yakovllm/**", "web/**", "Dockerfile"]
  workflow_dispatch:

jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Trigger Render deploy
        env:
          HOOK: ${{ secrets.RENDER_DEPLOY_HOOK }}
        run: |
          if [ -z "$HOOK" ]; then
            echo "RENDER_DEPLOY_HOOK is not set; skipping." >> "$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY"
            exit 0
          fi
          curl -fsS -X POST "$HOOK" > /dev/null
          echo "Render deploy triggered." >> "$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY"

chunks.title: keep-warm.yml
chunks.text:
name: Keep the server awake
# Render's free plan puts a server to sleep after 15 idle minutes, and waking it takes ~50 s:
# that was most of the wait on a first question. A ping every 10 minutes keeps it awake.
# (One always-on free service uses ~744 of the 750 free hours a month.)
on:
  schedule:
    - cron: "*/10 * * * *"
  workflow_dispatch:

jobs:
  ping:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 3
    steps:
      - run: curl -fsS -m 90 https://yakov-llm.onrender.com/api/health -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code} in %{time_total}s\n" || true

chunks.title: refresh.yml
chunks.text:
# Keeps yakov.LLM in step with GitHub: re-indexes new or changed projects,
# commits the new knowledge base and republishes the demo on GitHub Pages.
name: Refresh knowledge base
on:
  schedule:
    - cron: "17 */6 * * *"          # every 6 hours
  workflow_dispatch:                 # "Run workflow" button
  repository_dispatch:
    types: [project-updated]         # sent by a project's push (see docs/notify-yakov-llm.yml)
  push:
    branches: [main]
    paths: ["web/**", "scripts/build_demo.py"]   # republish the demo when the UI changes

permissions:
  contents: write
  pages: write
  id-token: write

concurrency:
  group: refresh
  cancel-in-progress: false

jobs:
  refresh:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment:
      name: github-pages
      url: ${{ steps.deploy.outputs.page_url }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          ref: ${{ github.event.repository.default_branch }}   # always the latest main, also on re-runs
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with: { python-version: "3.12" }
      - name: Sync with GitHub (only changed repos are re-indexed)
        env:
          GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
        run: python -m yakovllm.ingest --github "${{ github.repository_owner }}"
      - name: Commit the new knowledge base
        id: commit
        run: |
          if git diff --quiet -- data/kb.json; then
            echo "changed=false" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"; echo "No project changed."
          else
            git config user.name "yakov.LLM bot"
            git config user.email "41898282+github-actions[bot]@users.noreply.github.com"
            git add data/kb.json
            git commit -m "Update knowledge base from GitHub"
            # main may have moved while we were indexing: replay our commit on top, retry a few times
            for i in 1 2 3; do
              git pull --rebase -X theirs origin "${{ github.event.repository.default_branch }}" && git push && break
              sleep 5
            done
            echo "changed=true" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
          fi
      - name: Build the static demo
        run: python scripts/build_demo.py
      - uses: actions/configure-pages@v5
      - uses: actions/upload-pages-artifact@v3
        with: { path: dist }

chunks.title: yakov.LLM
chunks.text:
# yakov.LLM

**עוזר AI שמכיר את כל הפרויקטים שלי ב-GitHub.** שואלים אותו על הקוד, על החלטות התכנון או איך להריץ משהו, ומקבלים תשובה עם הפניה לקובץ ולשורות המדויקות. כשאני מוסיף פרויקט או דוחף שינוי, הוא מתעדכן לבד.

An AI assistant that knows every project in my GitHub account. Ask about the code, the design decisions or how to run something, and the answer cites the exact file and lines. When I add a project or push a change, it updates itself.

**▶ Live app:** https://yakov-ashgar27.github.io/yakov.LLM/ (installable on phone and desktop; search runs in the browser, written answers come from the hosted server)

![Home screen](docs/screenshot-home.png)

📐 **System design:** [DFD (levels 0–1) and data model](docs/DIAGRAMS.md), drawn from the code.

chunks.title: yakov.LLM › Where to look in the code
chunks.text:
## Where to look in the code

- [`yakovllm/search.py`](yakovllm/search.py): BM25 written from scratch, with field weighting, repo focus and per-file diversity.
- [`yakovllm/tokenizer.py`](yakovllm/tokenizer.py): one tokenizer for Hebrew and code. It splits `findPathStep` into its words and strips Hebrew prefixes (ו, ה, ב, ל…).
- [`yakovllm/facts.py`](yakovllm/facts.py): reads the code itself (Python with `ast`, JS/TS/Java with careful patterns) and writes a fact card for every function, class, API route and DB table, every file, and every project: dependencies, run commands, tests, CI, endpoints, settings.
- [`yakovllm/memory.py`](yakovllm/memory.py): remembers who it talked with and what they said, kept apart from the knowledge base as unverified notes.
- [`yakovllm/sync.py`](yakovllm/sync.py): follows a GitHub account and re-indexes only the repos that changed, then swaps the live index without a restart.
- [`web/engine.js`](web/engine.js): the same search engine in JavaScript, so the static demo needs no server. A test checks that both return identical results.
- [`eval/`](eval/): 38 questions with known answers, and the script that scores retrieval.

chunks.title: yakov.LLM › How it works
chunks.text:
## How it works ```mermaid flowchart LR GH[(GitHub account)] -->|new or changed repos| SYNC[sync.py
every 30 min / webhook / Action] SYNC --> CH[chunker.py
code, docs, pages
with line numbers] CH --> KB[(data/kb.json)] KB --> IDX[BM25 index
search.py] Q[Question] --> RW[Query rewrite
fast model] RW --> IDX IDX -->|top 6 excerpts| LLM[LLM: Groq, Gemini or Claude
answers with citations] LLM -->|streamed| UI[Chat UI] ``` 1. **Ingest.** Every text file that helps answer questions (source code, Markdown, HTML pages, config) is split into chunks that keep their repo, path and line range. Markdown is split by headings, code into 60-line windows that prefer to end on a blank line, HTML pages into visible text. Each repo also gets an overview chunk with its summary, file types and folders. 2. **Search.** A question is tokenized the same way and scored with BM25. Hebrew words are also mapped to the English words the code uses ("אויב" → `enemy`), because a Hebrew question about English code otherwise shares no words with it. With an API key, a fast model also suggests search keywords and probable function names. 3. **Answer.** The six best excerpts go to the model with the conversation, and the model must cite them as `[1]`, `[2]`. The model is pluggable: Claude, or free options (open models on Groq, Gemini Flash), or any OpenAI-compatible endpoint. In the UI each citation opens the cited lines, highlighted, with a link to the same lines on GitHub. 4. **Code facts.** Raw code answers questions asked in the code's words. People ask in their own words ("where is the password hashed?", "what does it depend on?", "who calls this?"), so every push also regenerates fact cards from the code: one per function, class, method, React component, API route and database table (signature, docstring, file and lines, what it calls, where it is used), one per file (role, definitions, imports), and a few per project (dependencies, how to run, tests and CI, endpoints, tables, environment variables, folder structure). There are about 5,000 cards across 11 projects. They are generated, never hand-written, so they can't go stale. 5. **Your files too.** Attach files or a whole folder (Word, PDF, PowerPoint, Excel, text, code). They are read into text (Office files in the browser, PDF on the server), searched with the same engine, and their best passages go to the model next to the project sources. So you can ask "which project fits this job description?".

chunks.title: yakov.LLM › How it works
chunks.text:
6. **Memory.** The app remembers who it talked with (a random id the browser keeps, plus a name if one is given) and their earlier questions, so a returning visitor is greeted with context. What people *claim* is stored as an unverified note for Yakov to review on `/admin.html`, and never becomes part of the knowledge base. A name from another device only reveals that someone by that name talked before, never what they said.
7. **A real chat app.** Answers reply in the language you write in (or the one you pick), and a reply of just "2" picks option 2 of the last answer. Sources stay folded under each answer. Long-press a chat to rename, pin, save or delete it; search all chats; temporary chats that are neither saved nor remembered; a profile with name and photo; standing instructions ("answer in 3 bullets"); 👍/👎; read aloud; voice typing; select text in an answer to ask about it; a "what do you remember about me?" screen with a delete button; drafts that survive closing the app. Zip files and very long pastes become attachments.
8. **Folders.** Like Projects in the big chat apps: a folder has a name, its own instructions and up to 200 files (lectures, exercises, PDFs, slides, a whole directory or a zip). Every chat opened in it answers from those files, and its chats live inside it. Folders and chats can be pinned.
9. **Every project, when asked.** "The data structures of all the projects" or "of all of them" pulls the best excerpts from each project in turn, so the answer covers every one instead of the three that happened to rank highest; naming four projects covers exactly those.
10. **Fast and thorough.** The model is asked to think as little as it allows (retrieval already did the hard work), gets fewer, tighter excerpts, and a ping every 10 minutes keeps the free server awake, so answers start in seconds. Answers are detailed and end with 2-3 numbered follow-ups you can tap or pick by number.
11. **Stay current.** See below.

chunks.title: yakov.LLM › Staying in sync with GitHub
chunks.text:
## Staying in sync with GitHub

There are three ways, and they work together:

| How | When it runs | Setup |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Server sync** | Every 30 minutes, and on demand from the projects panel | Set `GITHUB_USER` |
| **Webhook** | Instantly on every push to a repo that has the webhook | Payload URL `…/api/webhook/github`, content type JSON, secret = `WEBHOOK_SECRET` |
| **GitHub Action** ([`refresh.yml`](.github/workflows/refresh.yml)) | Every 6 hours, from the Actions tab, or from a push in any project | Nothing. For instant runs, copy [`docs/notify-yakov-llm.yml`](docs/notify-yakov-llm.yml) into a project |

Each sync lists the account's public repos and compares each repo's `pushed_at` time with the stored one. A new repo is cloned and indexed, a changed repo is pulled and re-indexed (only that repo), and a deleted or archived repo is dropped. If GitHub can't be reached, the old index keeps serving.

chunks.title: yakov.LLM › Results
chunks.text:
## Results

Retrieval measured on [38 questions](eval/questions.json) (20 in Hebrew, 18 in English) over 11 repos, 750 files and about 7,200 chunks. A question is a hit when the file that holds the answer is in the top results.

| Setup | Hit@1 | Hit@5 | MRR | Hit@5 Hebrew | Hit@5 English | ms/query |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| BM25 (plain tokens) | 45% | 76% | 0.57 | 75% | 78% | 1.0 |
| BM25 + Hebrew→English glossary | 50% | **89%** | **0.65** | **95%** | 83% | 1.4 |

The glossary raises Hebrew recall from 75% to 95%. These numbers don't include the model keyword rewrite, which needs an API key at evaluation time. `python eval/run_eval.py` prints the table and lists the misses.

chunks.title: yakov.LLM › Results › Everyday questions
chunks.text:
### Everyday questions

[`eval/question_bank.json`](eval/question_bank.json) holds the questions people actually ask about a project ("what is it?", "how do I run it?", "how many lines of code?", "what was hardest?", follow-ups like "and how do I run it?"), in Hebrew and English. They are asked about every project, 234 questions in all, plus 8 questions about the whole account. `python eval/run_bank.py` checks what the model gets to read:

| Check | Result |
| --- | --- |
| The project's fact sheet (summary, languages, lines of code, links) is in the context | 100% |
| Excerpts come from the project that was asked about | 100% |
| Follow-up questions stay on the project of the conversation | 100% |
| Questions about the whole account get the all-projects overview | 100% |

[`eval/run_symbols.py`](eval/run_symbols.py) generates questions about randomly sampled functions, classes and files, in Hebrew and English, often with the identifier written as words ("find path step"), and checks that the right file reaches the model: **93%** of 750 questions. The misses are names like `__init__` that are ambiguous by nature.

The bank isn't a list of canned answers. It checks that whatever is asked, the model reads the right project, so it can answer in its own words.

chunks.title: yakov.LLM › Run it
chunks.text:
## Run it

Python 3.10+ is all you need, with **no dependencies** to install.

```bash
git clone https://github.com/yakov-ashgar27/yakov.LLM && cd yakov.LLM
export GROQ_API_KEY=gsk_...              # free written answers (or ANTHROPIC_API_KEY / GEMINI_API_KEY)
python -m yakovllm                       # http://localhost:8000
```

Without any key the app still works: answers are the matching excerpts. Reading PDF attachments needs `pip install pypdf` (the Docker image has it); everything else is standard library.

Memory is kept in `.cache/memory.json`. A free host wipes its disk on each deploy, so to keep it, create a **private** repo and set `MEMORY_REPO=owner/name` and `MEMORY_TOKEN` (a fine-grained token with Contents read & write on that repo only). Set `ADMIN_TOKEN` to read it at `/admin.html`.

| Provider | Key | Cost | Default model |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Groq | `GROQ_API_KEY` | Free tier, no card | `openai/gpt-oss-120b` |
| Google Gemini | `GEMINI_API_KEY` | Free tier | `gemini-flash-latest` |
| Anthropic | `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` | Paid | `claude-sonnet-5-5` |
| Any OpenAI-compatible API | `LLM_API_KEY` + `LLM_BASE_URL` | Varies | set `LLM_MODEL` |

[![Deploy to Render](https://render.com/images/deploy-to-render-button.svg)](https://render.com/deploy?repo=https://github.com/yakov-ashgar27/yakov.LLM)

On Windows you can double-click `run.bat` instead (it reads `.env`). To use Docker, run `docker build -t yakov-llm . && docker run -p 8000:8000 --env-file .env yakov-llm`. Render deploys `render.yaml` in one click.

To index a different account, run:

```bash
python -m yakovllm.ingest --github <user>          # only new or changed repos
python -m yakovllm.ingest --github <user> --force  # rebuild everything
python -m yakovllm.ingest --local ~/code/my-repo   # local folders
```

Settings are in [`.env.example`](.env.example).

chunks.title: yakov.LLM › Tests
chunks.text:
## Tests

```bash
pip install pytest && python -m pytest -q
```

There are 50 tests. They cover the tokenizer, the chunker (line numbers must match the source exactly), BM25 ranking, and GitHub sync against real temporary git repos (add, update, remove, and network failure). They also cover the HTTP API against fake Claude and OpenAI-compatible servers that speak their streaming protocols, webhook signatures, rate limiting, CORS for the static demo, identical Python and JavaScript search results on every evaluation question, the fact extractor, reply language and numbered-option picks, temporary chats, feedback and "forget me", memory (recall, unverified notes, never touching the knowledge base, name-only recall across devices), attachments and Word/PowerPoint/Excel/PDF extraction, and guards that fail CI if Hit@5 drops below 80% or the auto-generated symbol questions drop below 90%.

chunks.title: yakov.LLM › Design decisions
chunks.text:
## Design decisions

- **BM25 instead of embeddings.** The corpus is small, about 7,000 chunks. Code questions use exact identifiers (`find_path_step`, `RBAC`), where keyword search is strong. BM25 runs in 1 ms with no model download, and it runs in the browser too. Cross-language recall, the usual weakness, is handled by the glossary and the query rewrite. The evaluation set is there to show when embeddings start to pay off.
- **Facts generated from code, not written by hand.** A hand-written FAQ goes stale on the next push and only covers the questions someone thought of. Cards extracted from the code cover every function and file and are rebuilt on every push.
- **What visitors say is never knowledge.** The knowledge base is built only from the repos. Visitor claims go to a separate store, marked unverified, for a human to judge.
- **Standard library only.** The server, the model streaming clients and the search engine have no dependencies (PDF reading is the one optional extra), so the project runs anywhere and is easy to read end to end.
- **One engine, two runtimes.** The JavaScript port lets the demo work as a single static file. A parity test keeps both runtimes in lockstep.
- **Grounded answers.** The prompt requires a citation for every claim about the projects and an honest "not in the sources". The UI makes each citation one click away from the real lines.

## API

| Method | Path | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| GET | `/api/health` | Mode, model, index size, sync status |
| GET | `/api/repos` | Indexed repos with summaries and last push |
| GET/POST | `/api/search?q=…&repo=…&k=…` | Raw search results with scores and matched terms |
| POST | `/api/chat` | `{messages, repo?, attachments?, visitor?, chat?}` → Server-Sent Events: `meta` (sources), `delta` (text), `done` |
| POST | `/api/extract` | File bytes (name in `X-Filename`) → `{text}` for Word, PowerPoint, Excel, PDF |
| POST | `/api/feedback` | `{visitor, chat, vote: up/down, question, answer}` |
| POST | `/api/memory/me`, `/api/memory/forget` | What it remembers about this visitor, and deleting it |
| GET | `/api/memory` | Visitors, questions and unverified notes (`Authorization: Bearer <ADMIN_TOKEN>`) |
| POST | `/api/sync` | Check GitHub now (with `SYNC_TOKEN` set, needs `Authorization: Bearer <token>`) |
| POST | `/api/webhook/github` | GitHub webhook (HMAC-SHA256 verified) |

chunks.title: yakov.LLM: Data Flow & Data Model › Data model
chunks.text:
## Data model

yakov.LLM has no relational database: both stores are JSON documents. The diagram shows their structure as entities, so it is clear what is kept and how the parts relate.

```mermaid
erDiagram
    REPO ||--o{ CHUNK : "split into"
    VISITOR ||--o{ QUESTION : "asked"
    VISITOR ||--o{ NOTE : "told (unverified)"

    REPO {
        string key PK "owner/name"
        string branch
        string commit "last indexed commit"
        datetime pushed_at
        string summary
        int files
        int loc
        json languages
        json facts "run commands, tests, CI, endpoints"
    }
    CHUNK {
        string id PK
        string repo FK
        string path
        int start "first line"
        int end "last line"
        string kind "code · doc · symbol · file · facts · config · page · overview"
        string title
        text text
    }
    VISITOR {
        string id PK "random id kept by the browser"
        datetime first
        datetime last
        json names
        json chats "last 50"
        json projects "question count per project"
    }
    QUESTION {
        datetime t
        string chat
        text text
        json projects
    }
    NOTE {
        datetime t
        string chat
        text text
        bool correction
        bool verified "always false until Yakov reviews"
    }
```

Visitor memory never feeds the knowledge base: what a visitor says is stored only as an unverified note. Each visitor keeps at most 40 questions and 60 notes.

"""Build the static demo: ONE self-contained HTML file with the knowledge base inside.

    python scripts/build_demo.py            # -> dist/index.html (+ dist/kb.json)
    python scripts/build_demo.py --embedded # no live refresh from GitHub (for sandboxed hosts)

The demo needs no server. Search runs in the browser (web/engine.js); answers
come from Claude when the page is opened inside Claude, otherwise the page shows
the best matching excerpts. GitHub Pages serves this file (see .github/workflows).
"""
import base64
import json
import re
import sys
from pathlib import Path

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent
WEB = ROOT / "web"
DIST = ROOT / "dist"


def main() -> None:
    html = (WEB / "index.html").read_text(encoding="utf-8")
    kb = (ROOT / "data" / "kb.json").read_text(encoding="utf-8")
    json.loads(kb)  # fail early on a broken file

    def inline_css(m):
        return "<style>\n" + (WEB / m.group(1)).read_text(encoding="utf-8") + "\n</style>"

    def inline_js(m):
        return "<script>\n" + (WEB / m.group(1)).read_text(encoding="utf-8").replace("</script", "<\\/script") + "\n</script>"

    html = re.sub(r'<link rel="stylesheet" href="([\w.]+)">', inline_css, html)
    html = re.sub(r'<script src="([\w.]+)"></script>', inline_js, html)
    icon = base64.b64encode((WEB / "icon.svg").read_bytes()).decode()
    html = html.replace('href="icon.svg"', f'href="data:image/svg+xml;base64,{icon}"')
    embedded = "--embedded" in sys.argv
    if embedded:  # sandboxed host (an artifact): no manifest, no service worker, no live refresh
        html = re.sub(r'\s*<link rel="manifest"[^>]*>|\s*<link rel="apple-touch-icon"[^>]*>', "", html)
        html = re.sub(r"kbUrl: '[^']*'", "kbUrl: ''", html)
        html = html.replace("window.YAKOV_CONFIG = {", "window.YAKOV_EMBEDDED = true;\n    window.YAKOV_CONFIG = {", 1)
    if embedded:  # a sandboxed host can't fetch kb.json next to the page: put it inside
        kb_script = "<script>window.YAKOV_KB = " + kb.replace("</", "<\\/") + ";</script>\n"
        html = html.replace("</head>", kb_script + "</head>", 1)

    DIST.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    (DIST / "index.html").write_text(html, encoding="utf-8")
    (DIST / "kb.json").write_text(kb, encoding="utf-8")
    if not embedded:  # installable app (PWA) files
        for name in ("manifest.webmanifest", "sw.js", "icon.svg", "icon-192.png", "icon-512.png",
                     "icon-maskable-512.png", "apple-touch-icon.png", "admin.html", "style.css"):
            (DIST / name).write_bytes((WEB / name).read_bytes())
    print(f"dist/index.html · {len(html.encode()) / 1e6:.1f} MB")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

chunks.text:
"""Split source files into chunks that keep their file path and line numbers.

Every chunk remembers where it came from (repo, path, first and last line), so
an answer can cite "bomberman/ai.py lines 24-58" and link straight to GitHub.
"""
from __future__ import annotations

import html
import re
from dataclasses import asdict, dataclass

CODE_WINDOW = 60      # lines per code chunk
CODE_OVERLAP = 8      # lines repeated between neighbouring code chunks
MD_TARGET = 1500      # characters per markdown chunk (soft)
MD_MAX = 2400         # a section longer than this is split by paragraphs
HTML_WINDOW = 40

DEF_RE = re.compile(
    r"^\s*(?:export\s+)?(?:default\s+)?(?:async\s+)?"
    r"(?:def|class|function|const|let|interface|type|enum)\s+([A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*)"
)
HEADING_RE = re.compile(r"^(#{1,4})\s+(.*)")


@dataclass
class Chunk:
    id: str
    repo: str
    path: str
    start: int          # 1-based first line
    end: int            # 1-based last line
    title: str          # heading path for docs, first definition for code
    kind: str           # "doc" | "code" | "page" | "config"
    text: str

    def to_dict(self) -> dict:
        return asdict(self)


def _kind_for(path: str) -> str:
    low = path.lower()
    if low.endswith((".md", ".txt", ".rst")):
        return "doc"
    if low.endswith((".html", ".htm")):
        return "page"
    if low.endswith((".yml", ".yaml", ".toml", ".json", ".ini", ".cfg", ".bat", ".sh")) or low.endswith("dockerfile") or "/dockerfile" in low:
        return "config"
    return "code"


def _strip_html(lines: list[str]) -> list[str]:
    """Visible text of an HTML page, one output line per input line."""
    joined = "\n".join(lines)
    # Drop script/style bodies but keep their newlines so line numbers stay true.
    joined = re.sub(r"(?is)<(script|style)\b.*?</\1>", lambda m: "\n" * m.group(0).count("\n"), joined)
    joined = re.sub(r"(?s)<!--.*?-->", lambda m: "\n" * m.group(0).count("\n"), joined)
    joined = re.sub(r"<[^>\n]*>", " ", joined)
    joined = html.unescape(joined)
    return [re.sub(r"\s+", " ", ln).strip() for ln in joined.split("\n")]

chunks.title: chunker.py › _chunk_markdown
chunks.text:
joined = "\n".join(lines)

    joined = re.sub(r"(?is)<(script|style)\b.*?</\1>", lambda m: "\n" * m.group(0).count("\n"), joined)
    joined = re.sub(r"(?s)<!--.*?-->", lambda m: "\n" * m.group(0).count("\n"), joined)
    joined = re.sub(r"<[^>\n]*>", " ", joined)
    joined = html.unescape(joined)
    return [re.sub(r"\s+", " ", ln).strip() for ln in joined.split("\n")]


def _chunk_markdown(repo: str, path: str, lines: list[str]) -> list[Chunk]:
    sections: list[tuple[str, int, list[str]]] = []  # (heading path, start line, lines)
    stack: list[str] = []
    cur: list[str] = []
    cur_start = 1
    in_fence = False
    for i, line in enumerate(lines, 1):
        if line.strip().startswith("```"):
            in_fence = not in_fence
        m = None if in_fence else HEADING_RE.match(line)
        if m:
            if any(s.strip() for s in cur):
                sections.append((" › ".join(stack), cur_start, cur))
            level = len(m.group(1))
            stack = stack[: level - 1] + [m.group(2).strip().strip("*")]
            cur, cur_start = [line], i
        else:
            cur.append(line)
    if any(s.strip() for s in cur):
        sections.append((" › ".join(stack), cur_start, cur))

    # Merge small neighbouring sections; split very long ones by paragraph.
    chunks: list[Chunk] = []
    buf: list[str] = []
    buf_start, buf_title = 1, ""

    def flush(end_line: int) -> None:
        nonlocal buf
        text = "\n".join(buf).strip()
        if text:
            chunks.append(Chunk("", repo, path, buf_start, end_line, buf_title or path, "doc", text))
        buf = []

    for title, start, sec in sections:
        sec_text = "\n".join(sec)
        if len(sec_text) > MD_MAX:
            if buf:
                flush(start - 1)
            # paragraph split, still tracking line numbers
            para: list[str] = []
            p_start = start
            for j, ln in enumerate(sec):
                para.append(ln)
                size = sum(len(x) + 1 for x in para)
                if (not ln.strip() and size >= MD_TARGET) or size >= MD_MAX:
                    buf, buf_start, buf_title = para, p_start, title
                    flush(start + j)
                    para, p_start = [], start + j + 1
            if para:
                buf, buf_start, buf_title = para, p_start, title
                flush(start + len(sec) - 1)

BIDI_RE = re.compile("[\u200e\u200f\u202a-\u202e\u2066-\u2069\ufeff]")


def chunk_file(repo: str, path: str, content: str) -> list[Chunk]:
    content = BIDI_RE.sub("", content)
    lines = content.replace("\r\n", "\n").replace("\r", "\n").split("\n")
    kind = _kind_for(path)
    if kind == "doc" and path.lower().endswith(".md"):
        chunks = _chunk_markdown(repo, path, lines)
    elif kind == "page":
        chunks = _chunk_lines(repo, path, lines, kind, _strip_html(lines), HTML_WINDOW)
    else:
        chunks = _chunk_lines(repo, path, lines, kind, lines, CODE_WINDOW)
    for i, c in enumerate(chunks):
        c.id = f"{repo}:{path}:{c.start}-{c.end}"
    return chunks

chunks.title: dialog.py › reply_language
chunks.text:
"""Small conversation rules that a weak model gets wrong on its own.

* reply_language: answer in the language of the user's latest message ("Yes" -> English,
  "כן" -> Hebrew); a message with no letters ("2") keeps the language of the one before.
* resolve_choice: when the previous answer offered numbered options and the user replies with
  just a number ("2", "option 2", "אפשרות 2", "the second one"), that reply means the option's text.
web/app.js has the same rules for the in-browser mode.
"""
from __future__ import annotations

import re

HEBREW = re.compile(r"[א-ת]")
LATIN = re.compile(r"[A-Za-z]")
ORDINALS = {
    "first": 1, "second": 2, "third": 3, "fourth": 4, "fifth": 5, "last": -1,
    "ראשון": 1, "הראשון": 1, "ראשונה": 1, "הראשונה": 1, "שני": 2, "השני": 2, "שנייה": 2, "השנייה": 2, "שניה": 2,
    "השניה": 2, "שלישי": 3, "השלישי": 3, "שלישית": 3, "השלישית": 3, "רביעי": 4, "הרביעי": 4, "רביעית": 4,
    "הרביעית": 4, "אחרון": -1, "האחרון": -1, "האחרונה": -1,
    "אחת": 1, "אחד": 1, "שתיים": 2, "שתים": 2, "שלוש": 3, "ארבע": 4, "one": 1, "two": 2, "three": 3, "four": 4,
}
PICK = re.compile(
    r"^\s*(?:the\s+)?(?:(?:option|choice|number|no\.?|#|אפשרות|מספר|סעיף|את|ה|בחרתי(?: ב)?|i choose|i pick|let'?s go with|go with)\s*)?"
    r"([0-9]{1,2}|[א-תa-z']+)(?:\s*(?:one|please|בבקשה|תודה|אחד|אחת))?\s*[.!)]?\s*$", re.I)
LIST_ITEM = re.compile(r"^\s*(?:[-*]\s*)?(\d{1,2})[.)]\s+(.+)$")


def reply_language(messages: list[dict]) -> str:
    for m in reversed(messages):
        if m.get("role") != "user":
            continue
        text = str(m.get("content", ""))
        he, en = len(HEBREW.findall(text)), len(LATIN.findall(text))
        if he >= 2:  # Hebrew writers mix in English terms ("ה-API של guardstream"); English writers don't mix in Hebrew
            return "Hebrew"
        if en:
            return "English"
    return "Hebrew"


def numbered_options(text: str) -> list[str]:
    """The last numbered list in a message: ["Joint angles in real time — how ...", ...]."""
    groups: list[list[tuple[int, str]]] = []
    current: list[tuple[int, str]] = []
    for line in str(text).split("\n"):
        m = LIST_ITEM.match(line)
        if m:
            n = int(m.group(1))
            if current and n != current[-1][0] + 1:
                groups.append(current)
                current = []
            current.append((n, m.group(2)))
        elif line.strip() and current and not line.startswith((" ", "\t")):
            groups.append(current)
            current = []
    if current:
        groups.append(current)
    groups = [g for g in groups if len(g) >= 2 and g[0][0] == 1]
    if not groups:
        return []

Word / PowerPoint / Excel files are zip archives of XML, read with the standard library.
PDF needs pypdf (installed in the Docker image); without it PDFs are refused with a clear message.
"""
from __future__ import annotations

import io
import re
import zipfile

def _docx(z: zipfile.ZipFile) -> str:
    root = ET.fromstring(z.read("word/document.xml"))
    out = []
    for p in root.iter(W + "p"):
        style = p.find(f"{W}pPr/{W}pStyle")
        text = "".join(t.text or "" for t in p.iter(W + "t"))
        if not text.strip():
            continue
        level = re.match(r"Heading(\d)", style.get(W + "val", "")) if style is not None else None
        out.append(("#" * int(level.group(1)) + " " if level else "") + text)
    for tbl in root.iter(W + "tbl"):
        for row in tbl.iter(W + "tr"):
            cells = ["".join(t.text or "" for t in c.iter(W + "t")).strip() for c in row.iter(W + "tc")]
            if any(cells):
                out.append(" | ".join(cells))
    return "\n".join(out)


def _pptx(z: zipfile.ZipFile) -> str:
    slides = sorted((n for n in z.namelist() if re.match(r"ppt/slides/slide\d+\.xml$", n)),
                    key=lambda n: int(re.search(r"(\d+)", n.rsplit("/", 1)[-1]).group(1)))
    out = []
    for i, name in enumerate(slides, 1):
        root = ET.fromstring(z.read(name))
        paras = ["".join(t.text or "" for t in p.iter(A + "t")) for p in root.iter(A + "p")]
        paras = [p for p in paras if p.strip()]
        notes = f"ppt/notesSlides/notesSlide{i}.xml"
        if notes in z.namelist():
            nroot = ET.fromstring(z.read(notes))
            n = " ".join(t.text or "" for t in nroot.iter(A + "t")).strip()
            if n and not n.isdigit():
                paras.append(f"(notes) {n}")
        out.append(f"## Slide {i}\n" + "\n".join(paras))
    return "\n\n".join(out)

JAVA_CLASS = re.compile(r"^\s*(?:public\s+|private\s+|protected\s+|final\s+|abstract\s+)*(?:class|interface|enum|object)\s+([A-Z]\w*)", re.M)
JAVA_METHOD = re.compile(r"^\s+(?:@\w+\s+)*(?:public|private|protected|static|final|override|suspend|fun|\s)+[\w<>\[\],.? ]*?\b([a-z]\w*)\s*\(([^)]*)\)\s*(?::\s*[\w<>?]+\s*)?(?:throws [\w, .]+)?\s*\{", re.M)


def java_symbols(path: str, text: str) -> tuple[list[dict], dict]:
    lines = text.split("\n")
    syms = []
    for m in JAVA_CLASS.finditer(text):
        start = _line_of(text, m.start(1))
        syms.append({"name": m.group(1), "qual": m.group(1), "kind": "class", "start": start,
                     "end": _block_end(lines, start), "sig": lines[start - 1].strip()[:200],
                     "doc": _jsdoc_before(text, m.start()), "calls": [], "owner": None, "routes": []})
    owner = syms[0]["name"] if syms else None
    for m in JAVA_METHOD.finditer(text):
        if m.group(1) in NOT_METHODS:
            continue
        start = _line_of(text, m.start(1))
        syms.append({"name": m.group(1), "qual": f"{owner}.{m.group(1)}" if owner else m.group(1), "kind": "method",
                     "start": start, "end": _block_end(lines, start), "sig": lines[start - 1].strip()[:200],
                     "doc": _jsdoc_before(text, m.start()), "calls": [], "owner": owner, "routes": []})
    imports = re.findall(r"^\s*import\s+([\w.]+)", text, re.M)[:20]
    return syms, {"imports": imports, "doc": ""}

def build(paths: list[tuple[Path, str]], out: Path, owner: str = "") -> dict:
    repos, chunks = [], []
    for path, name in paths:
        meta, cs = ingest_repo(path, name)
        repos.append(meta)
        chunks.extend(cs)
    return write_kb(repos, chunks, out, owner)


ACCOUNT_PATH = "(all projects)"


def account_chunk(repos: list[dict], owner: str) -> dict | None:
    """One chunk about the whole account: every project, newest first, with dates, stack and size.
    Answers "which projects does Yakov have?", "what is the newest one?", "what does he use?"."""
    if not repos:
        return None
    ordered = sorted(repos, key=lambda r: r.get("pushed_at") or r.get("committed_at") or "", reverse=True)
    home = next((r["key"] for r in repos if r["key"] == (owner or "").lower()), ordered[0]["key"])
    lines = [f"# All projects of {owner} on GitHub / כל הפרויקטים של יעקב ב-GitHub",
             f"{len(repos)} projects (פרויקטים), newest first (מהחדש לישן). Portfolio, skills, technologies, experience.", ""]
    for r in ordered:
        loc = sum((r.get("loc") or {}).values())
        langs = ", ".join(list((r.get("loc") or {}).keys())[:4]) or ", ".join(list((r.get("languages") or {}).keys())[:4])
        when = (r.get("pushed_at") or r.get("committed_at") or "")[:10]
        lines.append(f"- {r['title']} ({r['key']}), last updated {when}: {(r.get('summary') or r.get('description') or '')[:220]}"
                     f" Stack: {langs}. {loc:,} lines of code." + (f" Live: {r['homepage']}" if r.get("homepage") else ""))
    return {"id": f"{home}:{ACCOUNT_PATH}:1-1", "repo": home, "path": ACCOUNT_PATH, "start": 1, "end": 1,
            "title": "All projects › overview", "kind": "overview", "text": "\n".join(lines)}

def write_kb(repos: list[dict], chunks: list[dict], out: Path, owner: str = "") -> dict:
    owner = owner or next((r["owner"] for r in repos if r.get("owner")), "")
    chunks = [c for c in chunks if c.get("path") != ACCOUNT_PATH]
    acc = account_chunk(repos, owner)
    if acc:
        chunks = [acc] + chunks
    kb = {
        "version": KB_VERSION,
        "owner": owner,
        "built_at": time.strftime("%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ", time.gmtime()),
        "repos": repos,
        "tokenizer": {  # shared with web/engine.js
            "stopwords": sorted(tokenizer.STOPWORDS),
            "glossary": tokenizer.GLOSSARY,
            "aliases": tokenizer.repo_aliases(repos),
            "prefix1": "".join(sorted(tokenizer.HE_PREFIX_1)),
            "prefix2": sorted(tokenizer.HE_PREFIX_2),
        },
        "chunks": chunks,
    }
    out.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    out.write_text(json.dumps(kb, ensure_ascii=False, separators=(",", ":")), encoding="utf-8")
    log(f"wrote {out} · {len(repos)} repos · {len(chunks)} chunks · {out.stat().st_size / 1e6:.1f} MB")
    return kb


def main(argv: list[str] | None = None) -> None:
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="Build the yakov.LLM knowledge base")
    ap.add_argument("--github", metavar="USER", help="ingest every public repo of this GitHub user")
    ap.add_argument("--repo", nargs="*", default=[], metavar="OWNER/NAME", help="specific GitHub repos")
    ap.add_argument("--local", nargs="*", default=[], metavar="DIR", help="local folders (git checkouts)")
    ap.add_argument("--out", default=str(DEFAULT_OUT))
    ap.add_argument("--force", action="store_true", help="with --github: re-index every repo, not only changed ones")
    a = ap.parse_args(argv)

    if a.github and not a.repo and not a.local:
        from .sync import GitHubSync  # full, incremental GitHub sync
        result = GitHubSync(a.github, Path(a.out)).check(force=a.force)
        print(json.dumps(result))
        if "error" in result:
            sys.exit(1)
        return
    targets: list[tuple[Path, str]] = []
    for full in a.repo:
        targets.append((clone(full), full.split("/")[-1]))
    for d in a.local:
        p = Path(d).expanduser().resolve()
        targets.append((p, p.name))
    if not targets:
        ap.error("give --github USER, --repo OWNER/NAME or --local DIR")
    build(targets, Path(a.out), owner=a.github or "")

"""BM25 search over the knowledge base, written from scratch (no libraries).

BM25 scores a chunk higher when it contains the query's rare words many times,
and normalises for chunk length. On top of plain BM25 we add three things that
matter for a code + docs corpus:

* field weighting: words in the repo name, file path and section title count
  as if they appeared META_WEIGHT times;
* repo focus: when the question names a project ("in Bomberman ..."), chunks
  from that project get a boost (or a hard filter when the UI picks a project);
* diversity: at most MAX_PER_FILE chunks from one file in the results, so the
  answer can draw on several places.
"""
from __future__ import annotations

import json
import math
import re
from collections import Counter, defaultdict
from dataclasses import dataclass
from pathlib import Path

from . import tokenizer

K1 = 1.2
B = 0.75
META_WEIGHT = 3
REPO_BOOST = 3.0       # the question names the project
CONTEXT_BOOST = 1.8    # the conversation so far was about the project
README_BOOST = 1.15
TEST_PENALTY = 0.8    # test files echo the code's words; prefer the code unless tests are asked about
TEST_WORDS = {"test", "tests", "pytest", "vitest", "בדיקה", "בדיקות", "e2e", "playwright"}
MAX_PER_FILE = 2
CARD_KINDS = {"symbol", "file"}   # fact cards about a file get their own per-file budget beside its code
FACTS_PATH = "(project facts)"
PER_PROJECT = 2       # excerpts per project when a question covers many projects
# "all the projects", "of all of them", "each project": the answer must cover every project
ALL_PROJECTS = re.compile(r"כל ה?פרויקטים|כל אחד מה?פרויקטים|בכל אחד|לכל אחד|של כולם|כולם|לכולם|בכולם|בכל ה?פרויקטים|"
                          r"\ball (?:the |my |of the |of his |his )?(?:projects|repos|repositories)\b|\b(?:every|each) (?:project|repo)\b|"
                          r"\ball of them\b|\bfor each\b|\bacross (?:all )?(?:the )?projects\b", re.I)


def wants_all(text: str) -> bool:
    return bool(ALL_PROJECTS.search(text or ""))


@dataclass
class Hit:
    chunk: dict
    score: float
    terms: list[str]

        """The excerpts a chat answer is written from.

        1. Work out which project(s) the question is about: the one picked in the UI, else the ones
           the question names, else the ones the conversation was about.
        2. Search, keeping only those projects (other projects only fill in if too little is found).
        3. Pin the project's fact sheet (summary, languages, lines of code, folders, links) and the
           start of its README, which answer most everyday questions: what it is, why, how to run it,
           what it's built with. With no project in play, pin the all-projects overview instead.
        """
        named = self.detect(query)
        if not repo and (wants_all(query) or len(named) > 3):
            return self.per_project_context(query, named if len(named) > 3 else self.project_keys(), extra_terms)
        targets = [repo] if repo else (named or list(context_repos or []))
        targets = targets[:3]
        if targets:
            pool = self.search(query, k=60, extra_terms=extra_terms, context_repos=targets)
            hits = [h for h in pool if h.chunk["repo"] in targets][:k]  # the fact sheet below covers thin matches
        else:
            hits = self.search(query, k=k, extra_terms=extra_terms)
        wanted: list[str] = []
        if targets:
            for t in targets[:2]:
                wanted.append(f"{t}:(overview):1-1")
                wanted.append(f"{t}:{FACTS_PATH}:1")
                readme = sorted((c for c in self.chunks if c["repo"] == t and c["path"].lower() == "readme.md"),
                                key=lambda c: c["start"])
                wanted += [c["id"] for c in readme[:2]]
        else:
            wanted += [c["id"] for c in self.chunks if c["path"] == "(all projects)"][:1]
            owner = (self.kb.get("owner") or "").lower()
            wanted += [c["id"] for c in self.chunks if c["repo"] == owner and c["path"].lower() == "readme.md"][:1]
        have = {h.chunk["id"] for h in hits}
        pinned = [Hit(self.by_id[i], 0.0, []) for i in dict.fromkeys(wanted) if i in self.by_id and i not in have]
        return pinned + hits

    def project_keys(self) -> list[str]:
        """Real projects, newest first: not the profile README, not one-file repos."""
        owner = (self.kb.get("owner") or "").lower()
        repos = [r for r in self.kb["repos"] if r["key"] != owner and (r.get("files") or 0) > 1]
        repos.sort(key=lambda r: r.get("pushed_at") or r.get("committed_at") or "", reverse=True)
        return [r["key"] for r in repos]

OWNER_NAME = os.environ.get("OWNER_NAME", "Yakov Ashgar")
STARTED = time.time()

class State:
    """The live index. Sync swaps it under a lock; requests read a reference."""

    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self.lock = threading.Lock()
        self.index = Index.load(KB_PATH) if KB_PATH.exists() else Index({"repos": [], "chunks": []})
        self.sync: GitHubSync | None = None

    def swap(self, kb: dict) -> None:
        new = Index(kb)
        with self.lock:
            self.index = new


STATE = State()


class RateLimiter:
    def __init__(self, limit: int, window_s: int = 600):
        self.limit, self.window = limit, window_s
        self.hits: dict[str, deque] = defaultdict(deque)
        self.lock = threading.Lock()

    def allow(self, key: str) -> bool:
        now = time.time()
        with self.lock:
            q = self.hits[key]
            while q and now - q[0] > self.window:
                q.popleft()
            if len(q) >= self.limit:
                return False
            q.append(now)
            return True


LIMITER = RateLimiter(int(os.environ.get("RATE_LIMIT", "30")))
MEMORY: Memory | None = None
MAX_ATTACH = 10
MAX_ATTACH_CHARS = 3500


def memory() -> Memory:
    global MEMORY
    if MEMORY is None:
        MEMORY = Memory.from_env()
    return MEMORY

chunks.title: Yakov Ashgar · יעקב אשגר › About me
chunks.text: ## About me - 🎓 Third-year **B.Sc. in Information Systems, AI specialization**, University of Haifa (graduating 2027–28). - 🛠️ I work across the **whole lifecycle**: requirements and data model (user stories, DFD, ERD), architecture, code, tests, CI and a live deployment. Each data-driven project has its DFD and ERD next to the code. - 📏 My projects report **measured results**, not just feature lists: detection rates, retrieval accuracy, statistical power, real-hardware validation. - 🪖 Former **combat soldier and commander, Haruv Reconnaissance Unit**. Still on active reserve duty, with 5 deployments completed alongside my studies. > 💡 **Short on time?** Ask [**yakov.LLM**](https://yakov-ashgar27.github.io/yakov.LLM/), an AI assistant I built that has read all my repositories. It answers questions about any project and cites the exact file and lines. --- ## ⭐ Featured projects

chunks.title: Yakov Ashgar · יעקב אשגר › ⭐ Featured projects › [🏋️ FitVision AI](https://github.com/yakov-ashgar27/fitvision-ai)
chunks.text: ### [🏋️ FitVision AI](https://github.com/yakov-ashgar27/fitvision-ai) **Final degree project · team of 4 · my role: lead full-stack developer** The phone camera tracks the trainee's skeleton, counts reps and corrects technique in real time. Trainers get analytic progress reports. - Pose estimation runs **on the device** (Web Worker): video never reaches the server. - Full spec: 20 user stories, DFD, ERD and a normalized **17-table** schema, RBAC. - Offline-first sync via IndexedDB; **66 tests** in CI on **SQLite, PostgreSQL and SQL Server**. `React PWA` `MediaPipe` `FastAPI` `SQL Server / PostgreSQL` `Redis + RQ` **[▶ Live app](https://fitvision-ai-naoj.onrender.com)** · [📐 DFD & ERD](https://github.com/yakov-ashgar27/fitvision-ai/blob/main/docs/04-%D7%A0%D7%99%D7%AA%D7%95%D7%97-%D7%95%D7%AA%D7%9B%D7%9F.md) · [Code](https://github.com/yakov-ashgar27/fitvision-ai)

chunks.title: Yakov Ashgar · יעקב אשגר › ⭐ Featured projects › [💰 FeatureLedger](https://github.com/yakov-ashgar27/FeatureLedger-Feature-P-L-Safe-Deprecation-Radar)
chunks.text: ### [💰 FeatureLedger](https://github.com/yakov-ashgar27/FeatureLedger-Feature-P-L-Safe-Deprecation-Radar) **SaaS product · FinOps for product teams · solo** Gives every product feature a monthly **profit & loss** statement (engineering effort from Git, support load, cloud and LLM spend against usage and ARR), then safely retires the features that lose money. - **Token-Bleed Radar** finds AI features whose LLM costs eat their revenue. - **Safe Sunset:** a guarded state machine that drives the feature flag, opens the dead-code PR itself and keeps a hash-chained audit log. - Multi-tenant with **Postgres Row-Level Security**, OIDC SSO, RBAC; **170+ tests**; ledger checked to the cent in CI. `FastAPI` `PostgreSQL 16 + pgvector` `Next.js 15` `Docker` `GitHub Actions` **[▶ Run in 1 click (Codespaces)](https://codespaces.new/yakov-ashgar27/FeatureLedger-Feature-P-L-Safe-Deprecation-Radar?quickstart=1)** · [📐 DFD & ERD](https://github.com/yakov-ashgar27/FeatureLedger-Feature-P-L-Safe-Deprecation-Radar/blob/main/docs/DIAGRAMS.md) · [Code](https://github.com/yakov-ashgar27/FeatureLedger-Feature-P-L-Safe-Deprecation-Radar)

chunks.title: Yakov Ashgar · יעקב אשגר › ⭐ Featured projects › [📂 DocMind](https://github.com/yakov-ashgar27/DocMind)
chunks.text: ### [📂 DocMind](https://github.com/yakov-ashgar27/DocMind) **Personal document assistant · web, Android and server · solo** *"I need the documents for my reserve-duty benefits."* DocMind finds what you already have, remembers what each process requires, and helps you get what's missing. - On-device **Hebrew/English OCR** and classification into 30 document types. - Security by design: **AES-256-GCM** per-file keys, RSA-3072 PIN vault, two-step verification. Documents stay on your own phone or server. - Phone and server editions share one knowledge base; CI proves they classify identically. **~80 tests**. `Python` `FastAPI` `Tesseract OCR` `WebCrypto` `PWA` `Android` **[▶ Open the app](https://yakov-ashgar27.github.io/DocMind/app/)** · [Android APK](https://yakov-ashgar27.github.io/DocMind/DocMind.apk) · [📐 DFD & ERD](https://github.com/yakov-ashgar27/DocMind/blob/main/docs/DIAGRAMS.md) · [Code](https://github.com/yakov-ashgar27/DocMind)

chunks.text: ### [📊 PulsePort Analytics](https://github.com/yakov-ashgar27/PulsePort-Analytics) **Product analytics & statistics · solo** Funnels, A/B tests and AI-model evaluations on your own data, with the statistical test behind every claim and a clear **GO / NO-GO** verdict. - Stops teams from shipping noise: flags a "+2.9% win" with p = 0.18 as **KEEP RUNNING** (63% power). - Frequentist + Bayesian A/B, FDR control, segment-level drop-off detection. - SciPy engine and an in-browser TypeScript port that agree in **22 parity test groups**. Data never leaves the browser. `Python` `SciPy` `FastAPI` `PostgreSQL 16` `React` `TypeScript` **[▶ Live app](https://yakov-ashgar27.github.io/PulsePort-Analytics/)** · [📐 DFD & ERD](https://github.com/yakov-ashgar27/PulsePort-Analytics/blob/main/docs/DIAGRAMS.md) · [Code](https://github.com/yakov-ashgar27/PulsePort-Analytics)

chunks.text: ### [🤖 yakov.LLM](https://github.com/yakov-ashgar27/yakov.LLM) **AI / retrieval-augmented generation · solo** An AI assistant that has read every one of my repositories. Each answer cites the exact file and lines, and it re-indexes itself when I push. - **BM25 search engine written from scratch**, with one tokenizer for both Hebrew and code. - Fact cards generated from the code (via `ast`) for every function, class, route and table. - Measured: the right file reaches the model for **89%** of test questions and **93% of 750** auto-generated ones. CI fails if accuracy drops. `Python (zero dependencies)` `JavaScript` `LLM APIs` `SSE streaming` `GitHub Actions` **[▶ Try it](https://yakov-ashgar27.github.io/yakov.LLM/)** · [📐 DFD & data model](https://github.com/yakov-ashgar27/yakov.LLM/blob/main/docs/DIAGRAMS.md) · [Code](https://github.com/yakov-ashgar27/yakov.LLM) --- ## ⚡ Real-time systems & networking

game states
Seven states, and every path leads back to the menu.
MENU PLAYING PAUSED PLAYER_DIED LEVEL_COMPLETE GAME_OVER VICTORY
two algorithms that make it smart
The enemy hunts you with BFS
Breadth-first search finds the first step on the shortest path to the player, around walls and bombs.
queue = deque([(start, None)])
while queue:
pos, first = queue.popleft()
for d in Direction:
nxt = step(pos, d)
if nxt == goal: return first or d
if walkable(nxt) and nxt not in seen:
seen.add(nxt)
queue.append((nxt, first or d))
Chain reactions with a queue
Every bomb a flame touches joins the queue, and each bomb explodes exactly once.
queue = list(due_bombs)
while queue:
bomb = queue.pop()
if bomb in done: continue
done.append(bomb)
for tile in flame_path(bomb):
other = bomb_at(tile)
if other and other not in done:
queue.append(other)

quality
84 pytest tests, headless – no window needed
~95% coverage of the game-logic code
5 levels, each validated when loaded
13 slide presentation, plus SRS and work plan
Tests cover game logic, enemies, bombs, levels, high scores, sound synthesis, translations and right-to-left text.
Every tunable value – speeds, timers, scores – lives in one config file.
The work plan split the team into four roles: management & spec, game logic, enemies & levels, and interface & quality.
key insights
Separate logic from display Keeping Pygame out of the rules made the core testable, and turned the renderer into a thin layer that is easy to change.
Tests alongside the code Writing tests in parallel with each module, not at the end, kept the last weeks free for user testing and polish.
Data over hard-coding Levels are plain text files and constants live in one place, so the game can grow without touching the engine.
Engineering is more than code A spec, a plan with roles and a presentation are what make a team project deliverable on time.

Final project · University of Haifa
FitVision AI
A web information system that watches a workout through the phone camera, coaches technique in real time, and turns every set into an analytical progress report for the trainer.
▶ Live demo
Source code
The demo runs on a free server that sleeps when idle, so the first load takes about 30 seconds.
Project Final project · University of Haifa
Team 4 students · Scrum
My role Lead full-stack developer
Status MVP live · field-tested
the idea
The problem
Many people train without a coach next to them, at home or in an open gym. They repeat exercises with poor form and get no objective feedback, which raises the risk of injury. Trainers, on their side, have no systematic way to follow trainees remotely and rely on what the trainee reports.
The solution
Pose detection in the browser, straight from the phone camera
Rep counting and form feedback on screen and by voice, as you train
Every workout logged at the set, rep and error-event level
Automatic reports, trends and alerts for the trainer
Video never leaves the phone – only numbers reach the server

chunks.title: fitness-tracker.html
chunks.text:
my role
I was the lead full-stack developer, responsible for the system architecture and the database. In practice that meant owning the server side and the design documents behind it:
Architecture Overall system design, chapter 4 of the specification: DFD (levels 0 and 1), ERD, business rules and the permission model.
Database A normalized 17-table SQL Server schema, versioned with Alembic migrations.
API The FastAPI server: authentication with JWT, role-based access control for trainees, trainers and admins.
Reports engine Automatic post-workout reports with trends, exported to RTL PDF and Excel by background workers.
how it works
The heavy work happens on the trainee's phone. The server only receives the numeric results of each set, which keeps the system fast and private by design.
Trainee phone React PWA
MediaPipe Pose 33 body landmarks per camera frame, in a Web Worker
Technique engine joint angles, rep counting, rule checks
Live coach skeleton overlay, counter, voice cues
↓ HTTPS · set data as JSON only – no video
Server Python · FastAPI
API gateway JWT authentication and an RBAC check on every request
Core services users, plans, sessions, sets, reps, errors
Reports engine metrics, trends, PDF & Excel in the background
Alerts engine daily scheduled job, alerts to the trainer
↓ SQLAlchemy · cache & queue · email

counting a rep
A rep is a state machine over a joint angle, not a single threshold. This is what stops noise and half-reps from being counted. Example: the knee angle in a squat.
Standing start / end of a rep
angle drops below 150°
Down checks descent rules
below the 100° depth threshold
Bottom records the lowest angle
rises 10° from the minimum
Up checks ascent rules
above 160° → rep +1
Going back up without reaching the bottom is a partial rep and is not counted. All thresholds live in the database (TechniqueRules), so each exercise can be tuned without changing code.

data model
Seventeen normalized tables, in five groups. The core is a strict hierarchy: a session holds sets, a set holds reps, and every form mistake is stored as an event on the rep where it happened. That level of detail is what makes the trainer reports possible.

the app
Trainee screens on the phone: home, camera setup and the live workout with skeleton overlay and form alerts. The interface is in Hebrew, right to left.
Trainer dashboard on desktop
testing with a real user
After the MVP was built we ran it on a real Android phone and read the results straight from the database. The data showed problems that no test on paper had caught:
What the data showed What we changed
A squat set logged 10 reps, but 3 were noise – twitches of 200–300 ms when entering the frame. A movement shorter than 0.6 s, or one that doesn't go 10° past the threshold, is no longer counted.
In bicep curls not a single rep passed – the thresholds were too strict for a side-view camera. Recalibrated 50° → 75° and 20° → 35°, shipped as a database migration, not a code release.
The same correction repeated on every frame, even after it was fixed. A coaching layer: one cue per rule per rep, rotating phrasings, plus "go all the way down" prompts and milestones.
From 2–3 meters away the on-screen text was hard to read. Voice feedback on by default, in Hebrew or English, with a short sound for every good rep.

engineering
17 database tables
66 automated tests in CI
3 databases tested: SQL Server, PostgreSQL, SQLite
0 frames of video sent to the server
Works offline: a workout is saved on the phone in IndexedDB and syncs automatically when the network is back.
Installable: a PWA for phones, tablets and laptops, including iPhone and iPad.
Deployed: every push to main redeploys the app to Render, with PostgreSQL on Neon.
key insights
Privacy is an architecture decision Running pose detection on the device meant the server never needs video. That one choice solved privacy, bandwidth and server cost together.
Rules belong in data, not code Storing technique thresholds as database rows turned the post-trial recalibration into a migration, and lets an admin add exercises without a developer.
Real users beat assumptions One session on a real phone exposed noise, wrong thresholds and unreadable screens. Reading the raw data showed exactly where to fix.
Let constraints pick the tools Hebrew PDFs ruled out WeasyPrint, so reports print through Chromium. Slow report jobs moved to a Redis queue to keep the API fast.
what's next
Accuracy Validation against 40 labeled videos, with a target of at least 95% rep-count accuracy and 85% recall on form errors for every exercise.
Pilot A pilot with 5 trainers and 15 trainees, aiming for a SUS usability score of 70 or more.
Exercises More exercises beyond the four in the MVP (squat, lunge, bicep curl, shoulder press) – added as data through TechniqueRules.
Showcase Live demo, poster and presentation at the department's project conference, June 2028.

The Map Lies
“The map always lies. The only question is about what.” A grid-based puzzle-stealth game where the minimap you rely on is deliberately wrong – and every level is mathematically guaranteed to be solvable without guessing.
▶ Play in the browser
Source code
Installable as an app on Windows, Mac, Android, iPhone and iPad, and playable offline. Hebrew by default, English one click away.
Type Puzzle-stealth web game
Stack React 19 · TypeScript · Vite
Levels 5 hand-made + endless procedural
Verified 500 generated levels per test run
the idea
How it plays
You crawl through a pitch-black dungeon with a lantern that lights only the 3×3 tiles around you. A minimap in the corner shows the whole level – but it hides one or more deliberate lies. Compare what the lantern shows with what the map claims, and click the tile to call out the lie.
What makes it work
Catch every lie and the fog lifts and the map “confesses”
Disguised traps punish players who trust the map blindly
From level 5 the map gets angry : it glitches near an uncaught lie, but never says where
All sound is synthesized live with the Web Audio API – no audio files

chunks.title: the-map-lies.html
chunks.text:
five kinds of lies
Lie The map says Reality
Phantom Wall Wall Open floor – often a hidden shortcut
Illusion Floor Open path Solid wall, a dead end
Disguised Trap Safe floor or a treasure chest A lethal spike trap
Fake Exit Exit in room A The real exit is in room B
Relocated Treasure Chest in room A The real chest is in room B
the level generator
Every endless-mode level comes from a seeded random generator, so the same seed always builds the same dungeon. One attempt runs five stages:
Carve A recursive-backtracker maze on odd coordinates.
Open up Knock out ~10% of walls for loops, then carve 1–3 rooms.
Place Exit on the safe tile farthest from the start, by BFS; chests in dead ends.
Inject lies Draw N lies, spaced apart and away from the start.
Validate Accept only if every rule passes; otherwise retry with the next seed.
zero-guessing validator
The hard part of a game built on lies is fairness: a player must always be able to deduce a lie, never guess it. Every level – generated or hand-made – must pass five invariants, all checked with BFS on the true grid:
R1 · Reachability A trap-free path from start to the real exit always exists.
R2 · Observability Every lie is inside the lantern’s view from some reachable tile.
R3 · No blind steps Every trap is visible one step before you could stand on it.
R4 · Deducible Each lie creates a contradiction the player can actually see.
R5 · Bookkeeping Map and truth differ only at declared lies – no accidental ones.

chunks.title: the-map-lies.html
chunks.text:
R4 · Deducible Each lie creates a contradiction the player can actually see.
R5 · Bookkeeping Map and truth differ only at declared lies – no accidental ones.
proof, not hope
500 generated levels validated on every run (100 levels × 5 seeds)
~0.5 ms average generation time, under 10 ms worst case
≤ 3 attempts any level has ever needed
0 runtime dependencies besides React
The test script also feeds the validator deliberately broken levels – a choke-point trap, an undeclared difference, a sealed-off lie – and checks it rejects each one.
It checks that generation is deterministic and that the game rules behave as specified.
GitHub Actions runs the verification and the build on every push, then deploys to GitHub Pages.
key insights
Fairness has to be provable A game about lies is only fun if the lies are fair. Writing the rules down as invariants turned “feels fair” into something a test can check.
Generate, then validate Instead of a generator that is clever enough to never fail, a simple generator plus a strict validator and retry is easier to trust and to change.
Test the tester Feeding the validator broken levels on purpose proves it actually catches the problems it claims to.
Seeds make bugs reproducible Because every level comes from a seed, any strange level can be replayed exactly with ?seed= and ?level= .

AI project · retrieval-augmented generation
yakov .LLM
A portfolio is a stack of repositories that nobody has time to read. So I built a reader that never gets tired: an AI assistant that has gone through every line I have pushed to GitHub, answers questions about it in Hebrew or English, and points to the exact lines behind each answer. And when I push a change, it reads that too.
▶ Ask it something
Code
Works in the browser and installs as an app on phone and desktop. Try “How does the Bomberman enemy find the player?” and click the number next to the answer.
Type AI assistant · RAG
Stack Python · JavaScript · LLM APIs
Knows Every repo on my GitHub, 600+ passages
Running cost $0 (free tiers)
the idea
The problem
A recruiter opens my GitHub for a minute and a half. In that time they can't learn why the Bomberman enemy uses breadth-first search, how FitVision counts a squat, or why The Map Lies never forces a guess. All of that is in the code, but nobody will dig for it.
The answer
Ask anything about my projects, in Hebrew or English
Every claim in the answer carries a number like [2]
Click it, and the exact lines open with a link to them on GitHub
If the code doesn't say, it says so. No made-up features
Attach a job description, a CV or a whole folder, and it connects them to the projects
Feels like a real chat app: it answers in your language, remembers you, and lets you pin, rename, search and edit

chunks.title: yakov-llm.html
chunks.text:
from question to cited answer
Read Follow my GitHub account and pull every repo: code, docs, pages and config.
Split Cut files into passages that remember their repo, path and line numbers.
Search Rank the passages for the question with a BM25 engine I wrote from scratch.
Write A language model drafts the answer from the top passages only, streamed word by word.
Cite Each claim links to its passage, so the reader can check the source instead of trusting the model.
a search engine from scratch
I could have used a vector database and an embedding model. For about 7,000 passages full of exact identifiers like find_path_step or RBAC , plain keyword ranking is faster, needs no model download, and is easy to explain. The interesting part was making it understand both of my languages:
Code-aware findPathStep also counts as find , path and step , and chase_range as chase and range .
Hebrew-aware Hebrew glues words together: “והאויבים” also searches for “האויבים” and “אויבים”.
Bilingual A Hebrew question about English code gets English search terms: “אויב” brings in enemy , “רודף” brings in chase .
Fair ranking Words in file names and headings weigh more, test files step back unless you ask about tests, and no single file can fill the whole answer.
# BM25: rare words that appear often in a short passage score highest
score += idf(term) * tf * (K1 + 1) / (tf + K1 * (1 - B + B * length / avg_length))
it reads the code, not just the words
People don't ask in the code's words. They ask "who calls this?", "what does it depend on?", "how do I run it?". So on every push yakov.LLM reads the code itself and writes a fact card for everything in it. Nothing is written by hand, so nothing goes stale.
Every function and class Its signature, docstring, file and lines, what it calls and where it is used. Python is parsed with ast ; JavaScript, TypeScript and Java with careful patterns.
Every file Its role, what it defines and what it imports.
Every project Dependencies, run commands, tests and CI, API endpoints, database tables, settings and folder structure.
Tested at scale 750 auto-generated questions about random functions and files, in Hebrew and English. 93% reach the right file; the misses are names like __init__ that are ambiguous by nature.
it remembers, carefully
Talk to it today and come back next week, and it remembers what you asked about. What visitors tell it is a different matter: a claim from a stranger is not a fact about my code.
Separate from knowledge The knowledge base is built only from the repos. What people say goes to a separate store, marked unverified, for me to read.
A name proves nothing On the same device it recalls the whole conversation. Someone on another device who uses the same name only hears that a person by that name talked before, never what was said.

chunks.title: yakov-llm.html
chunks.text:
Separate from knowledge The knowledge base is built only from the repos. What people say goes to a separate store, marked unverified, for me to read.
A name proves nothing On the same device it recalls the whole conversation. Someone on another device who uses the same name only hears that a person by that name talked before, never what was said.
it keeps itself up to date
A portfolio assistant that forgets my latest work is worse than none. yakov.LLM compares every repo's last push time with what it already knows, and re-reads only what changed. There are three ways it hears about a change:
Every 30 minutes The server checks my GitHub account and swaps in the new index without a restart.
On every push A webhook with a signed secret can trigger a sync within seconds.
Every 6 hours A GitHub Action rebuilds the knowledge base and republishes the app.
The first surprise On its very first run, it found a new project on my account and read its code. The project was yakov.LLM itself.
measured, not guessed
I wrote 38 questions with known answers, 20 in Hebrew and 18 in English, and score the search over all 11 projects on every change. A question is a hit when the file that holds the answer is in the top five results.
89% of questions find the right file in the top 5
75→95% Hebrew questions, before and after the bilingual glossary
<1 ms per search, in Python or in the browser
50 automated tests, plus guards that fail CI if accuracy drops
The same search engine runs in Python on the server and in JavaScript in the browser. A test runs both on every question and requires identical results.
The server has no dependencies : the HTTP server, the streaming model client and the search engine all use only the standard library.
The model is pluggable: Gemini and Groq on free tiers, Claude , or any OpenAI-compatible API. Without any key it still answers with the matching passages.
key insights
Retrieval is the product The model can only be as right as the passages it gets. Measuring the search did more for answer quality than any prompt tweak.
Citations build trust An answer you can check in one click is worth more than a longer one you have to believe.
Simple beats fashionable BM25 plus a small bilingual glossary beat my expectations for code questions. The evaluation set will say when embeddings start to pay off.
Build with AI, verify like an engineer I built yakov.LLM with Claude as a pair programmer. The tests, the evaluation set and the parity check are how I made sure that what we built actually works.

Python (standard library) BM25 RAG Gemini · Groq · Claude APIs Server-Sent Events Vanilla JavaScript PWA & service worker GitHub Actions GitHub Pages Docker · Render Python ast Word · PDF · PowerPoint parsing pytest · Playwright

chunks.title: ⚓ PulsePort Analytics › The problem
chunks.text:
## The problem

Digital teams make product decisions from dashboards every day. Three mistakes recur, and each one is expensive:

| Mistake | What it looks like | What it costs |
|---|---|---|
| **Shipping noise** | "Variant B is up 3%, ship it!" The test is underpowered and *p = 0.18*. | Roll-outs of features that do nothing, or harm, and a team that stops trusting experiments. |
| **Averages hide the problem** | The overall funnel looks fine, while mobile users in one market abandon at twice the rate. | Revenue leaks silently at the highest-intent step. |
| **Choosing AI on vibes** | An LLM is picked from a few impressive answers, without confidence intervals, hallucination rates or cost per ticket. | Over-paying for accuracy that isn't significantly better, or deploying a model that fabricates answers. |

Most tools stop at charts. **PulsePort turns data into decisions:** every insight comes with the statistical test behind it, a correction for multiple comparisons, and a plain-language recommendation.

chunks.title: ⚓ PulsePort Analytics › What it does
chunks.text:
## What it does

PulsePort answers three questions for any digital product: a booking portal, an online store, a SaaS app, a bank.

1. **Where are we losing users, and who exactly?** An ordered funnel analysis tests every segment *and segment pair* (e.g. *country × device*) at every step against everyone else. It controls the false-discovery rate, estimates lost conversions, and detects when latency predicts abandonment.
2. **Did the change actually work?** A/B analysis runs frequentist and Bayesian inference side by side. It adds a sample-ratio-mismatch check, Fisher's exact test for small samples, Holm correction for more than two variants and a pre-registered power rule. The result is an explicit **GO / NO-GO / KEEP RUNNING / STOP** verdict that **prevents false-positive roll-outs**.
3. **Which AI assistant should we deploy?** Model evaluation reports scores with confidence intervals, hallucination rates against a safety guardrail, P95 latency, cost per 1,000 tickets, and significance tests between models.

It works in two modes:

| | **Data Studio** (public site) | **Full platform** (self-hosted, `docker compose up`) |
|---|---|---|
| Data in | CSV upload, paste from Excel or Sheets, Google Sheet / CSV link | Plus PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, Google Analytics 4, server-side CSV |
| Engine | TypeScript port of the stats engine, **verified against SciPy** | Python / SciPy engine + analytical SQL on PostgreSQL 16 |
| Privacy | Runs entirely in the browser; nothing is uploaded | Credentials stay on your server, with read-only queries |
| Cost | Free (GitHub Pages) | Free (open source, your own machine) |

chunks.title: ⚓ PulsePort Analytics › What it does › Example: what it finds on the bundled e-commerce sample
chunks.text:
### Example: what it finds on the bundled e-commerce sample

> 🔴 **country × device = BR · mobile under-performs at checkout_start → payment**: 32.6% pass vs 64.4% for everyone else (−31.8 pp, FDR q < 0.0001). Closing the gap is worth ≈24 conversions in the period.
> 🔴 **Slower checkout load predicts abandonment** at checkout_start → payment: r = −0.23, Holm-adjusted p < 0.0001.
> 🟢 Desktop out-performs at product_view → add_to_cart (+4.0 pp, q = 0.008).

And on an A/B test with a +2.9% lift (p = 0.18):

> 🟡 **KEEP RUNNING**. Inconclusive, so do not roll out yet. The test has only 63% power to detect a +5% effect, and P(B>A) = 90.9% is suggestive but not conclusive. About 48 more days are needed at current traffic.

---

chunks.title: ⚓ PulsePort Analytics › Data Studio: bring your own data
chunks.text:
## Data Studio: bring your own data

| Step | What happens |
|---|---|
| **1. Connect** | Upload a CSV, paste a table copied from Excel or Google Sheets, or connect a **Google Sheet / public CSV URL**. Re-connect any time to refresh with live data. |
| **2. Detect & map** | Columns are profiled (id, timestamp, category, number, boolean) and the dataset type is detected. Every mapping can be changed, and any column names work. |
| **3. Analyse** | The same statistics as the Python engine run **in your browser**, verified against SciPy on 22 test groups. |
| **4. Act** | Insights are ranked by severity and business impact. Export a Markdown report or a CSV of the results. |

**Supported datasets**

| Type | Minimum columns | What you get |
|---|---|---|
| **Event log / funnel** | session or user id, event name (optional: timestamp, latency, up to 3 segment columns) | Ordered funnel. Every segment **and segment pair** is tested at every step against everyone else, with Benjamini–Hochberg FDR control and an estimate of lost conversions. You also get the latency ↔ abandonment link (Holm-adjusted), a daily trend with a 7-day MA, and a week-over-week change alert. |
| **Funnel, aggregated** | step, users (optional: segment columns) | The same diagnostics from counts, e.g. a GA4 export or a `GROUP BY` result. Warns when counts aren't nested. |
| **A/B test, per user** | variant, converted 0/1 (optional: numeric metric, timestamp, segments) | Sample-ratio-mismatch check, z / χ² / **Fisher exact** for small samples, Katz CI, Holm correction for more than two variants, Beta-Binomial P(B>A) and expected loss, power at your MDE, days remaining, Mann-Whitney and Welch on the metric, effect reversals by segment, and a verdict. |
| **A/B test, summary** | variant, users, conversions | The same, from aggregated counts. |
| **AI evaluation log** | model, score (optional: hallucination flag, latency, cost, category) | Mean score with t-CI, Wilson CI on hallucination, Kruskal-Wallis, Welch on the top two, χ² on safety, a category leaderboard, a cost trade-off and a guardrail verdict. |

Five sample datasets ship with the app: a shipping portal, an **e-commerce checkout**, an A/B test per user, an A/B summary and an AI evaluation log. Anyone can try it in one click.

---

chunks.text:
## Connect your data sources (self-hosted, free)

In the self-hosted version, the **Your Data → Database / GA4** tab connects directly to:

| Source | How it connects | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **PostgreSQL** | asyncpg | Any SELECT / WITH query. Templates for event logs, A/B tests and AI logs. |
| **MySQL / MariaDB** | aiomysql | Same. |
| **SQLite** | aiosqlite, opened read-only | Put files in `connectors/data/`. |
| **Google Analytics 4** | Official Data API (free quota) | Users per event × country / device / channel, analysed as an aggregated funnel. |
| **CSV URL** | Fetched by the server | Works when the browser would be blocked by CORS. |

**Safety model**
- **Two layers of read-only protection.** First, a static check accepts only a single SELECT / WITH statement. Second, **every query runs inside a `READ ONLY` transaction with a timeout**, so the database itself refuses writes. CI proves the second layer separately on real PostgreSQL and MySQL, with the first layer disabled.
- **Row cap.** Results are limited to `PULSEPORT_CONNECTOR_MAX_ROWS` (default 500k).
- **Passwords.** They are sent only to your own server and never stored. To keep credentials off the browser entirely, use **saved connections**:
  ```bash
  PULSEPORT_CONNECTIONS='{"warehouse":{"type":"postgres","host":"host.docker.internal","database":"analytics","user":"readonly","password":"…"}}'
  PULSEPORT_ALLOW_ADHOC_CONNECTIONS=false   # only saved connections can be used
  ```
- **Path restriction.** SQLite files are opened only from `connectors/data/`, and paths are traversal-checked.
- **Reaching your own machine.** A database running on your own computer is reachable from Docker as `host.docker.internal`.
